 1      Introduction
For σ > 0, a metric space (M, dM ) is said to admit a σ-separating random partition if for
every ∆ > 0 there is a distribution over random partitions of M into clusters of diameter at
most ∆ with the property that for every two points x, y ∈ M the probability that x and y
belong to distinct clusters is at most σ/∆ times the distance between x and y. The smallest
σ for which this is possible is called the separation modulus of M and it is denoted SEP(M).

           Separating random partitions are a well studied clustering primitive which was introduced
       and investigated in [10] (precursors that considered it implicitly, with a variety of applications,
       appear in [49, 7, 1, 40]); see e.g. [54, 55] for more on the history. By [10], every n-point
       metric space (M, dM ) satisfies SEP(M) = O(log n), and there are metric spaces for which
       this bound is sharp. In [45], a randomized polynomial time algorithm was designed that takes
       as input a finite metric space (M, dM ) and outputs a factor 2 approximation to SEP(M).
       See [11, 20, 41, 31, 46, 24, 47, 45, 8, 54, 55, 43, 56, 44, 57] for an indication of the literature
       on this topic. The investigation of separating random partitions of finite-dimensional normed
       spaces, which is what we study herein, originates in [58], motivated by applications to network
       routing and distributed computing. The work [20] sharpened and generalized the bounds
       of [58], and influenced later research, e.g. [47, 4, 55]; similar partitioning schemes appeared
       implicitly in the earlier work [37] on SDP-based algorithms for graph colorings. Applications
       of separating random partitions to pure mathematics have also been found, notably to metric
       embeddings [11, 24, 56] and extension of vector-valued Lipschitz functions [47, 55].
